explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Jesus says, “…and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you.” So the measure you use on others has everything to do with it. I'm going to check my own measuring cup before I go near yours.

That's right, friend. Jesus says, “For with the same judgment you pronounce, you will be judged, and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you.” The two are tied together. Whatever measuring cup you pick up for somebody else, I think you'd better like it.

Beam is it, friend! Jesus puts a speck in your brother's eye next to a beam in your own. A beam. In your EYE. I've done some silly things in my day, but nobody ever walked into my bakery wearing lumber on their face.

I see why a tear came to mind, since eyes do water. But Jesus doesn't say tear. He sets a speck against a beam, and the huge size gap is the whole picture. A tear wouldn't make anybody stop and look at themselves.

A lash is a nice small guess, friend, but Jesus goes much bigger. He says the thing you don't notice in your own eye is a beam. The speck is the small one, and the beam is the big one. Picture that in your eye and tell me you wouldn't notice.

explanations.answer: Take the beam out of your own eye
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jesus says, “First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye.” Notice He says first. Clean up your own side, then your view gets a whole lot clearer.

Close, but that's not quite where Jesus lands. He says the beam comes out of your own eye first, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye. So the speck still has a plan. It just waits until you can see.

Asking forgiveness is a kind thing, friend, but it isn't what Jesus says here. Right after “You hypocrite!” He says, “First take the beam out of your own eye…” That's the first job, and your own eye is where it happens.

True, baker! Jesus says, “…and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye.” Beam out first, then clear sight. I wish my own mornings worked that well before coffee, and I don't even drink coffee.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says that once the beam is out of your own eye, “you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother's eye.” So He isn't saying never help. He's saying see clearly first.

That's the one, baker. Jesus says that if you throw your pearls before swine, “they may trample them under their feet…” He is talking about something valuable being treated as if it's worth nothing. That's a hard thing to watch.

explanations.answer: They may be buried in the mud
explanations.explanation: Mud is a fair picture, friend, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says they may trample the pearls under their feet. Trampled, not buried. Same sad ending for a pearl, though.

explanations.answer: They may be carried off to a pen
explanations.explanation: That one wanders off a bit, friend. Jesus doesn't mention a pen anywhere in the verse. He says they “may trample them under their feet, and then turn and tear you to pieces.” Nobody carries anything off in this one.

Jesus actually says the opposite, friend. He says, “For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened.” Everyone, not some. I'd stack that promise up against any other promise out there.
Right, baker! Jesus says, “For everyone who asks receives…” Not some, not a few. The word is everyone, and He says the same about the one who seeks and the one who knocks.

Father is it, baker. Jesus says, “…how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!” He starts with people who are evil but still know how to give good gifts to their children. Then He says the Father in heaven gives far more.

Angels are impressive, friend, but they aren't who Jesus names. He says, “…how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!” The giver is the Father Himself. That's the whole comfort of the verse.

Prophets get a mention later in this very sermon, but not here. In verse 11 Jesus says it's your Father in heaven who gives good things to those who ask Him. He compares that Father to a parent who gives a child a good gift. So the Father is the one doing the giving.

You got it, baker! Jesus says, “In everything, then, do to others as you would have them do to you. For this is the essence of the Law and the Prophets.” That's a lot of Scripture packed into one sentence. I can't even fit a full batch on one tray.

Those are both wonderful books, friend, but Jesus doesn't name them here. He says treating others the way you'd want to be treated is “the essence of the Law and the Prophets.” That's the phrase to hold onto.

The temple is a big deal, but Jesus isn't talking about it in this verse. He says the rule about doing to others as you would have them do to you is “the essence of the Law and the Prophets.” It's all about how we treat people.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, “For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it.” It's a hard line, so I'll say it plainly. Wide and easy is not the same as safe.

Rest sounds good, friend, and a wide road does look roomy. But Jesus says the wide gate and the broad way lead to destruction. He says many enter through it. I think that's why He tells us to pick the other gate.

Life is a good word, but Jesus gives it to the other gate. He says, “…small is the gate and narrow the way that leads to life…” The wide gate and broad way lead to destruction. The two gates go to two very different places.
Almost, friend, but one word changes it. Jesus says the small gate and narrow way lead to life, then adds, “…and only a few find it.” Few, not many. The many are the ones going through the wide gate.
Right! The first half is true, because the small gate leads to life. But Jesus says, “…and only a few find it.” So the statement fails on the word many. Few find it.
Wolves, baker! Jesus says they come “in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.” A cozy sheep coat on the outside and a hungry wolf underneath. That's quite the costume.

Lions are certainly fierce, friend, but Jesus picks a different animal. He says the false prophets come in sheep's clothing but are “inwardly…ravenous wolves.” The wolf is the one hiding in the sheep outfit.

A bear would be hard to hide in a sheep suit, friend, so I get it. But Jesus says false prophets are inwardly “ravenous wolves.” Wolves look like they could slip into a flock. Sheep's clothing on the outside, wolf on the inside.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, “…every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit.” The tree and the fruit match. It's the simple rule Jesus gives for recognizing people.
Leaves are a creative guess, friend, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says a bad tree bears bad fruit. The tree still produces fruit, and it matches the kind of tree it is.
Little is close in spirit, but Jesus isn't talking about amount. He says, “…a bad tree bears bad fruit.” It's about the kind of fruit, not the size of the harvest.

Jesus says the opposite, friend. He says, “A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit.” Cannot. No exceptions mentioned. I've spent a lot of years around ovens, and I've never seen one hold a surprise.

Right, baker. Jesus says, “A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit.” He doesn't leave a loophole, so a good tree doesn't sometimes bear bad fruit. The fruit shows what kind of tree it is.

explanations.answer: It is cut down and thrown into the fire
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” It's a heavy line, and I won't dress it up. He is serious about the difference between good fruit and none.

explanations.answer: It is pruned and given another year
explanations.explanation: That sounds gentle, friend, but it isn't what this verse says. Jesus says every tree that doesn't bear good fruit “is cut down and thrown into the fire.” There's no extra year in this passage. It's a serious word.

explanations.answer: It is left to dry up in the field
explanations.explanation: Drying up is a quieter ending, friend, but Jesus describes something different. He says such a tree “is cut down and thrown into the fire.” Cut down, then the fire. I think that's meant to get our attention.

explanations.answer: The one who does His Father's will
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus says, “Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven.” Saying it isn't the whole thing. Doing the Father's will is what He names.

explanations.answer: The one who prays the longest
explanations.explanation: Long prayers feel impressive, friend, but Jesus doesn't measure by length. He says only “he who does the will of My Father in heaven” will enter. I once stood at my oven for an hour and the cookies still didn't bake themselves.

explanations.answer: The one who knows the most Scripture
explanations.explanation: Knowing Scripture is a good thing, friend, but that isn't what Jesus names in this verse. He says, “…only he who does the will of My Father in heaven.” The weight is on doing.

That's it, baker, and I think this one is heavy. Jesus says, “Then I will tell them plainly, 'I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!'” He says it to people who listed what they did in His name. Take a quiet moment with that one.
That would be a gentler ending, friend, but it's not what Jesus says here. He says He will tell them plainly, “I never knew you…” It's a heavy verse, and I won't make it lighter than it is.
Waiting would give a bit more room, friend, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says, “I never knew you; depart from Me…” It's a heavy moment, and it follows what they said on that day.
True, baker, and it's a heavy one. Jesus says, “I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!” Both parts are right there in verse 23. It's a sobering line.
This one is true, friend. Jesus says, “…depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!” Both the name and the command are in the verse. It's a heavy verse, so I'll just let it stand.
That's right, baker. Jesus says the wise man “built his house on the rock.” Everyone who hears His words and acts on them is like that man. The foundation is the whole story.
A hilltop sounds like a smart spot, friend, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says the wise man built his house on the rock. It's the foundation that matters, not the view.
A riverside house sounds scenic, friend, but that's not the picture. Jesus says the wise man “built his house on the rock.” Where the house sits is the rock, plain and simple.
Not this one, friend. Jesus says the rain fell, the torrents raged and the winds blew, “yet it did not fall…” The storm hits, but the house stands. That's what makes the picture so encouraging.

That's right, baker! Jesus says the rain fell, the torrents raged and the winds blew and beat against that house, “yet it did not fall…” The storm is real, and the house still stands. I'd like to meet that foundation.

explanations.answer: Its foundation was on the rock
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says it did not fall “because its foundation was on the rock.” It's not about how fancy the house looks. It's about what's underneath.

explanations.answer: Its walls were built extra thick
explanations.explanation: Thick walls sound sturdy, friend, but Jesus says nothing about the walls. He says the house stood “because its foundation was on the rock.” The reason is underneath it.

explanations.answer: Its roof was tied down tight
explanations.explanation: A tied-down roof sounds handy in a windstorm, friend, but Jesus doesn't mention it. The reason He gives is that its foundation was on the rock. The house stands because of what it sits on.

Foolish is right, baker! Jesus says everyone who hears His words and does not act on them “is like a foolish man who built his house on sand.” Hearing without acting is the problem. The wise man hears and acts.
Sand, baker! Jesus says the foolish man “built his house on sand.” Compare that with the rock the wise man chose. The ground is what makes all the difference.
Lazy is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word Jesus uses. He says the man who hears His words and doesn't act on them is a foolish man. The wise man and the foolish man are the two pictures.
Rock belongs to the other builder, friend. Jesus says the wise man built his house on the rock. The foolish man “built his house on sand.” Two builders, two foundations.
A hill sounds like a reasonable spot, friend, but Jesus doesn't mention one. He says the foolish man built his house on sand. The wise man's rock and the foolish man's sand are the two foundations.

explanations.answer: It falls with a great collapse
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus says the house “fell—and great was its collapse!” It's the same storm that the wise man's house stood through. This house just had a different foundation.
That would be a lucky ending, friend, but Jesus doesn't give it. He says the house “fell—and great was its collapse!” It doesn't lean and it doesn't stay up.
Losing just a roof would be a cheap fix, friend, but Jesus describes much more. He says the house “fell—and great was its collapse!” The whole house goes down.
Astonished, baker! Matthew writes that the crowds “were astonished at His teaching.” That's quite a reaction after a long sermon. Nobody on this hill was checking their watch.
Puzzled is understandable after so much teaching, friend, but that's not the word Matthew uses. He says the crowds were astonished at His teaching. They were amazed by it.
Offended might fit some sermons, friend, but Matthew doesn't say it here. He writes that the crowds were astonished at His teaching. Astonished is the word.

True, baker! Matthew says the crowds were astonished “because He taught as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.” The scribes were the teachers the crowds already knew. Jesus taught with authority.
This one is true, friend. Matthew writes that He taught “as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.” That's the reason the crowds were astonished. It's right there in verse 29.
